newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Peters welcomes o/seas investors if in NZ interest.
newsitem.headline: Peters welcomes o/seas investors if in NZ interest.

text.p: Treasurer Winston Peters said on Friday the New Zealand government welcomed foreign investment if it was in the national interest.
Peters' New Zealand First party campaigned in last year's general election for tighter controls on foreign investment.

But he said in a speech to the American Chamber of Commerce luncheon in Auckland: "Let me be clear, this government is not opposed to foreign investment. When it is in the national interest we welcome all investment that boosts employment, productivity and growth.
"But if we can increase our savings there is likely to be less reliance on the savings of others to fund our future," Peters said.
NZ First formed a centre-right coalition with the conservative National Party last December.

"Although New Zealand (state) Superannuation will remain a key source of retirement income for New Zealanders, the government is looking to every New Zealander to make a contribution to their retirement and thus do their bit to increase national savings," Peters said.

A referendum will be held in September on a compulsory superannuation scheme that would require everyone to contribute a portion of income to an individual pension savings scheme -- initially three percent in 1998/99, rising to eight percent by 2002.
NZ First campaigned on the need for a compulsory scheme at the October election, but many prominent National MPs are opposed.

Peters said there was no definitive measure of whether New Zealand was saving enough, but there were partial indicators such as a balance of payments deficit, the fact much of the improvement in savings comes from government savings rather than private savings, and net external liabilities were increasing and totalled 80 percent of GDP. He said the nation needed to look at managing the impact of increased numbers of people in retirement which would see the ratio of potential workers to pensioners fall from 5.1 to one to 2.7 to one by the year 2031.
